sow.alignment: First of two dedicated Week 3 exemplars. Directly teaches selective breeding and its impact; genetic engineering is taught in the companion lesson. Foundation-relevant 4.8 and evaluation in 4.14; no claim to cover tissue culture.

safety: Paper and screen lesson; no live organisms, biological cultures or chemical work.
practicalAlternative: All evidence is supplied for offline use. Discuss, point, annotate or dictate instead of cutting cards or writing extended prose.

access.supported: Same scientific objective, with chunked cards, word bank, read-aloud access and short evidence stems. Accept accurately explained oral or annotated responses.
access.standard: Use two evidence sources and a reasoned explanation independently.
access.stretch: Evaluate limitations, explain a mechanism and transfer to unfamiliar evidence.
access.regulation: Offer solo or partner working and a quiet response route. Preview the sequence; allow a brief reset and re-entry at the next numbered task. No compulsory performance or timed competition.

title: Selective breeding: design a resilient crop
subtitle: Choose parents, inspect offspring, then improve the breeding decision
objective: Explain selective breeding and justify a breeding plan using inherited traits, performance evidence and genetic diversity.
priorLearning: Genes/alleles can be inherited; offspring from sexual reproduction vary.
A measured trait can be influenced by inherited factors and environment.
A mean summarises a set of values; larger numbers are not always better.
success: Sequence selection, reproduction, offspring testing and repeated selection.
Choose parents and offspring using both yield and damage evidence.
Explain why selected offspring still vary and why diversity matters.

vocabulary.meaning: Humans choosing which organisms reproduce to increase desired inherited traits over generations.
Useful crop produced; here, grain mass per plant.
Ability to limit damage from a particular disease or pest.
Variety of inherited genetic information in a population.
Breeding between close relatives, which can increase the chance of harmful recessive combinations.

equipment: Pupil breeding record and shared candidate table; pen or mini-whiteboard.
Projector/offline deck; optional counters to mark parent choices.
preparation: Print the shared evidence page and one response route. Table values are constructed sample data.
Read the programme rule: two parents, both disease-damage scores at most 2, at least one yield at least 45 g, different family lines where possible.
In this constructed example, yield and resistance have inherited components. No single dominant/recessive model is assigned to them.

misconceptions.claim: The best parent produces identical perfect offspring.
misconceptions.correction: Sexual offspring inherit combinations of alleles and can vary; environment also affects phenotype.
misconceptions.check: Ask why sibling Q can show more damage than its parents in the constructed results.

misconceptions.claim: Selective breeding changes a plant during its lifetime.
misconceptions.correction: Breeders choose reproduction; inherited characteristics may become more frequent over generations.
misconceptions.check: Ask which generation changes after the parent decision.

misconceptions.claim: The biggest yield number is always the best choice.
misconceptions.correction: A breeding objective can also require resistance, health and diversity.
misconceptions.check: Compare D with B/C using both columns and the rule.

misconceptions.claim: Breeding close relatives always causes disease.
misconceptions.correction: It increases certain risks; it does not guarantee a harmful outcome.
misconceptions.check: Ask pupils to replace “always” with a risk statement.

slides.title: Can a breeder improve two traits at once?
body: Mission: plan a productive, disease-resistant crop.
A good choice must use evidence and survive a second check.
slides.notes: Show the outcome and predict the trade-off: 'If I choose only the biggest yield, what might I miss?' Do not introduce competition or claim pupils are plant geneticists making actual release decisions. This is a paper breeding model.

slides.title: Retrieve inheritance
body: R1. What is an allele?
R2. Are sexual offspring always identical to their parents?
R3. Can growing conditions affect measured yield?
slides.notes: R1 a version of a gene. R2 no; offspring inherit combinations and vary. R3 yes, for example water/light/nutrients. If R2 is insecure, point to the later sibling table before pupils make selections. Accept accurate plain-language explanations.

slides.title: How selective breeding works
body: Humans decide which organisms reproduce.
Choose inherited traits, breed, compare offspring, select again.
Repeat across generations.
slides.notes: Think aloud through a crop goal: 'I want useful grain yield and lower disease damage. I compare candidates, select parents and breed them. I cannot order their offspring to be perfect, so I test offspring before choosing the next parents.' Describe variation as the reason selection is possible. The cycle is a model, not a one-lesson growing practical.

visual.title: Selective breeding changes later generations
visual.description: Four linked steps: choose parents for inherited traits, reproduce, compare varied offspring, and select for the next generation. The repeated cycle changes the breeding population; individual plants do not choose to change their genes.

slides.title: Inheritance is a mechanism
body: Offspring receive alleles from both parents.
A simple model can show inheritance.
Real yield and resistance can involve many genes.
slides.notes: Use the two-locus diagram only as a compact recap. Parent AABB contributes AB and aabb contributes ab, so AaBb receives alleles from both. Do not assign dominant yield or resistance labels to these letters; those complex traits are not a monohybrid cross. Say: 'This tells me how genetic information is passed on, not the exact crop yield.'

visual.title: Offspring are not photocopies
visual.description: Conceptual inheritance model using fictitious allele symbols at two loci. Parents AABB and aabb produce AaBb offspring. This shows transmission of alleles only: yield and disease resistance in the breeding activity are multi-gene traits, not assigned to these symbols.

elements.text: An allele can be inherited; a wish cannot

Symbol model only. Real yield and resistance
can involve many genes and the environment.

slides.title: Read change across generations
body: The population mean can shift after selection.
G0 to G3: 34 g to 44 g per plant.
A trend is not a guarantee for every plant.
slides.notes: Teacher model: 'The mean increased by 10 g from generation 0 to 3 in these constructed results. I should not say every plant improved or that selection alone is proved to cause the change. The trial conditions were held the same, but a comparison line would strengthen a causal claim.' Ask a pupil to locate G2 = 43 g.

visual.title: Selection can shift a population
visual.description: Constructed sample data: mean grain mass per plant is 34, 39, 43 and 44 g in generations 0 to 3, with the same trial conditions. This illustrates a possible outcome, not a guarantee that yield always rises or that every offspring improves.

elements.text: Constructed sample data: selected crop line
Mean grain mass per plant (g); matched conditions

slides.title: Protect useful variation
body: Repeated close-relative breeding can reduce diversity.
Some harmful recessive combinations become more likely.
Retain suitable unrelated lines and check offspring.
slides.notes: Shares the preceding 3-minute I do stage. Distinguish increased risk from certainty. Plant breeders may intentionally use inbred lines in particular programmes, but this school scenario prioritises diversity and resilience. Do not generalise family relationships to pupils or request examples from their families.

visual.title: Keep variation in the breeding population
visual.description: Two conceptual breeding plans: repeatedly select two close relatives, or include suitable unrelated lines. Less diversity can increase shared vulnerability. Different labels represent family lines, not a count of all genes.

elements.text: Select useful traits and protect diversity

Can reduce genetic diversity
and increase inbreeding risk.

Retain useful variation;
still test offspring carefully.

Neither plan guarantees health or future yield.
Family labels are a simplified model.

slides.title: Breeding round 1: choose the parents
body: W1. Both parents: damage at most 2.
At least one parent: yield at least 45 g.
Use different family lines. Choose and justify.
slides.notes: Use the displayed constructed table and the printed copy. Two minutes private/paired choice, then explain using both criteria. B and C meet the rule; B has damage2, C1 and C yield46. A and D fail damage despite high yield. These are choices between characterised breeding lines; the rule is deliberately strict to make an evidence-based decision possible.

table.caption: Constructed sample data: matched trial conditions; lower damage is better. Each line mean comes from 10 plants.

slides.title: Breeding round 2: respond to new evidence
body: W2. Offspring target: yield at least 45 g; damage at most 2.
W3. Choose its next partner: sibling P or unrelated E?
Justify the choice and one needed check.
slides.notes: Shares the preceding 7-minute We do. Reveal constructed offspring outcomes only after round1 decision. S has 50 g and damage2, so meets both traits and has the highest qualifying yield. E (45 g, damage1, unrelated F5) is a reasonable next partner to retain diversity rather than repeatedly breed close siblings. Accept P only with an explicit reason and acknowledgement of diversity risk; E is preferred under this programme. Re-test plants/offspring and use more samples before scaling up.

table.caption: Constructed sample data: P–S are siblings from B × C; E is from a separate suitable line. One trial per plant.

slides.title: What changes after selection?
body: A breeder repeatedly selects resistant plants.
Choose the best biological explanation.
slides.notes: Collect independent answers. If B is not selected, return to parents → inherited alleles → varied offspring → selection. The response must say population/generations, not a plant trying harder.

options.text: Each plant decides to change its genes.
options.feedback: Individuals do not intentionally change genes to meet the breeder’s goal.

options.text: Desired inherited traits can become more common in later generations.
options.feedback: Selected parents pass on alleles, and repeated selection can change the breeding population.

options.text: Every offspring has exactly the same traits.
options.feedback: Sexual offspring vary; outcomes must be tested.
Environment continues to affect crop performance.

slides.title: Write a two-generation breeding log
body: Use the shared candidate and offspring evidence.
Record selection, rejection and the reason for each.
Finish with a prediction and a test.
slides.notes: Offer one route only. Supported = short stems/selection table; Standard = two-generation decision log; Stretch = evaluate claimed success with comparison evidence. The product should allow another scientist to understand the decision, not merely name two letters. At minute4 ask 'Which criterion ruled one out?' At minute8 check the future test.

slides.title: A decision needs its evidence
body: I selected … because the table shows …
I rejected … because …
I would check … before the next generation.
slides.notes: Shares 11-minute independent stage. A TA may read the criteria and table aloud. Do not supply the chosen letters. Pupils may speak the log while someone records it. Stretch pupils should evaluate a control line and sampling, not simply write more.

slides.title: Do not promise a perfect crop
body: Predict a possible shift in the population.
Keep uncertainty about individual offspring.
Name a way to retain diversity.
slides.notes: Shares independent time. Correct 'all offspring will inherit both features' to 'some offspring may combine useful alleles, so we select after testing'. Mark explanations by content, not quantity of writing.

slides.title: Peer-check the breeding plan
body: Can your reader follow both selections?
Ask one question about a trait or risk.
Use the response to improve one decision.
slides.notes: Light Lundy loop: choice of partner or teacher audience; pointing/speaking/writing equally welcome; teacher uses one suggestion in the shared model. Sample question: 'Where did you account for damage rather than only yield?' Give time to revise.

slides.title: A strong breeding log
body: Names a valid selection with two data points.
Explains inheritance, variation and repeated selection.
Includes diversity and a practical next check.
slides.notes: Shares 3-minute review. Use three formative checks; this is not a board mark scheme. Explicitly praise a changed decision justified by new evidence, not certainty or competitiveness.

slides.title: Transfer the method
body: E1. Give the four main selective-breeding steps.
E2. Why test offspring before choosing again?
E3. Name one risk of repeatedly using close relatives.
slides.notes: E1 select parents, breed, test/compare offspring, repeat selecting suitable offspring. E2 they vary and environment affects performance. E3 reduced genetic diversity/increased chance of harmful recessive combinations or shared vulnerability. Accept precise short responses.

pupilPages.title: Shared evidence | Crop breeding programme
pupilPages.intro: All numbers below are constructed sample data for a paper model. Yield and resistance have inherited components; neither is controlled by a single gene in this activity.

blocks.text: Round 1 rule: choose two parents. Both must have disease damage at most 2. At least one must have mean yield at least 45 g per plant. Use different family lines. Lower damage is better; 0 = no visible damage, 10 = severe damage.
Constructed sample data above: each line mean represents 10 plants in matched trial conditions.
Round 2 target: yield at least 45 g and damage at most 2. P–S are siblings from the selected cross; E is from a separate family. Constructed single-plant observations from one matched trial.

blocks.prompt: W1. Parent choice and reasons. W2. Next offspring choice. W3. Its next partner and one check.

pupilPages.title: Supported route | Record the decisions
pupilPages.intro: Use the shared evidence. Say, write or dictate the same scientific explanation.

blocks.prompt: S1. Choose two first parents. Give one damage value for each and the qualifying yield value.
S2. Explain why A or D fails the programme rule even though it has high yield.
S3. Choose one offspring from P–S with high yield and low damage. Give both values.
S4. Choose sibling P or unrelated E as its next partner. Explain one reason and one limitation.
S5. Number the method in the correct order.
choices: Compare offspring and select useful ones.
Select parents with desired inherited traits.

blocks.prompt: S6. Finish: offspring still need testing because … .

pupilPages.title: Standard route | Two-generation breeding log
pupilPages.intro: Use exact evidence from the shared page. Your log should make the decisions reproducible.

blocks.prompt: M1. State the programme goal. Choose round 1 parents using three numerical values and family-line evidence.
M2. Reject one alternative parent with a specific reason. Why is yield alone insufficient?
M3. Use the offspring evidence to select a next-generation candidate and partner. Explain the genetic-diversity decision.
M4. Explain how repeatedly selecting suitable parents can change later generations. Include inheritance and variation.
M5. Predict one possible outcome and describe how you would test it fairly before extending the programme.

pupilPages.title: Stretch route | Does the programme work?
pupilPages.intro: Constructed sample data for a follow-up trial. Both lines used the same growing conditions; values are means of 10 plants. Selection line and comparison line began from the same mixed seed population.

blocks.prompt: T1. Calculate the G0–G3 change for each line and the difference between those changes. What does the comparison add?
T2. Evaluate: “Every plant improved by 10 g because breeding guarantees success.” Use the table and its limitations.
T3. Propose two improvements to the evidence before recommending this crop: one about sampling/trial design and one about diversity or disease.
T4. Choose S with E or S with P from the shared data. Defend the decision while acknowledging one trade-off.

pupilPages.title: Exit and reflection | Explain the mechanism
pupilPages.intro: Use short scientific statements. No family or medical examples are needed.

blocks.prompt: E1. Write the main four steps of selective breeding in order.
E2. Why test offspring before choosing the next parents?
E3. Name one risk of repeatedly breeding close relatives.
L1. What question did your audience ask? Which decision or explanation did you improve?
My next useful step is…
choices: Explain genetic diversity as a risk issue.

answers.label: R1–R3 retrieval
answers.answer: R1 an allele is a version of a gene. R2 no: sexually produced offspring inherit combinations and can differ from both parents. R3 yes: for example light, water, nutrient availability and temperature can affect yield.

answers.label: W1 / S1 / M1 first selection
answers.answer: B and C meet all round1 criteria: damage2 and1 (both at most 2), C mean yield46 g/plant (at least 45), and families F2/F3 differ. B’s yield40 does not disqualify it because the rule needs only one parent at or above45. Cite values with the relevant units.

answers.label: S2 / M2 rejecting alternatives
answers.answer: A (48 g but damage6) and D (52 g but damage8) each fail the damage criterion. High yield alone may leave a crop vulnerable in the model; programme success needs both traits. Their F1 family also means A × D would not preserve different family origins.

answers.label: W2 / S3 offspring decision
answers.answer: S has the highest yield among qualifying offspring (50 g, damage2). P also meets a45 g and damage≤2 target (45 g,1) and is defensible if prioritising lower damage; state the trade-off. Q has damage6; R has42 g, below45. Do not claim S is certain to breed true.

answers.label: W3 / S4 / M3 next partner
answers.answer: E is preferred under the diversity goal:45 g, damage1, separate F5 family, whereas P is an F4 sibling of S. E may help retain genetic diversity but does not guarantee healthy or high-performing offspring. Re-test candidates and test many offspring in matched conditions. Accept a argued S × P plan only if the pupil explicitly explains its useful traits and the close-relative risk.

answers.label: S5 sequence
answers.answer: Correct displayed choice order numbers: compare offspring =3; select parents =1; repeat =4; breed =2. Biological order: select desired inherited traits in parents, reproduce, compare/select offspring, repeat over generations.

answers.label: S6 / E2 variation
answers.answer: Sexual offspring inherit different allele combinations; traits can involve many genes and environmental effects. They need testing because not all combine the intended performance, as Q’s damage6 demonstrates.

answers.label: M4 mechanism
answers.answer: Selected parents pass alleles to offspring. Offspring vary. Choosing those with useful inherited traits to reproduce again can increase those alleles/traits in the breeding population across generations. Individuals do not alter their genes because they are selected.

answers.label: M5 prediction and fair test
answers.answer: Possible prediction: a later population may have more plants combining yield≥45 g with damage≤2. Test many offspring and a comparison population under the same light, water, soil and disease challenge, recording both traits; repeat trials. Avoid saying all offspring must improve. This is a proposed trial, not instructions to culture pathogens.

answers.label: T1 follow-up calculation
answers.answer: Selected line:44−34=10 g/plant. Comparison:36−34=2 g/plant. Difference between changes:8 g/plant. A contemporaneous comparison helps distinguish a selection-associated shift from changes affecting both lines. It does not remove all uncertainty or prove the mechanism alone.

answers.label: T2 evaluate success claim
answers.answer: A mean increase of10 g does not show every individual rose by10 g; individual values and spread are missing. Breeding does not guarantee outcomes. The comparison increased2 g, so factors beyond the selective programme may contribute. Replication, individual data and disease results are needed.

answers.label: T3 improved evidence
answers.answer: One trial design improvement: larger replicated plots, randomised positions, repeat seasons/sites or retain individual values/ranges. One diversity/disease improvement: measure several disease challenges, monitor genetic diversity or include suitable unrelated lines and compare their offspring. Explain how the improvement addresses uncertainty rather than merely saying “more accurate”.

answers.label: T4 trade-off
answers.answer: Preferred S × E combines useful observed performance and distinct family origins, reducing repeated close-relative pairing. Potential trade-off: offspring still vary; E’s observed yield45 is lower than S50, and a single trial may misrepresent inherited performance. S × P can be discussed with a clear close-relative risk and a testing plan.

answers.label: Hinge A–D
answers.answer: B is correct: later generations may contain more of the selected inherited traits. A implies purposeful mutation; C ignores variation; D ignores continuing environmental influences.

answers.label: E1 / E3 exit
answers.answer: E1 choose parents for desired inherited traits; breed them; compare and select offspring; repeat across generations. E3 accept reduced genetic diversity, greater probability of harmful recessive combinations, or shared vulnerability; do not accept that harm is guaranteed.

answers.label: L1 reflection and assessment
answers.answer: A useful revision adds an overlooked trait value, corrects inheritance language or addresses diversity. Success requires a justified selection, accurate multigeneration mechanism and risk-aware next check. Reading/writing confidence is not the assessment target.

teacherNotes: 40 minutes: opening2, retrieval3, I do10, We do7, hinge3, independent11, review3, exit1. Zero-minute slides share their stage time.
This activity is a paper model, not a practical protocol for plant infection, genetic modification or animal breeding. No live material is required.

The initial table describes breeding-line means, while the later table describes individual offspring. Teach this distinction explicitly; do not compare a line mean and an individual as if they had equal reliability.
Yield/resistance in the activity are complex traits. The AABB/aabb diagram demonstrates allele transmission only and does not assign yield/resistance to a simple dominant/recessive model.
Choose one response route. All routes preserve selection using evidence and the mechanism over generations; stretch adds evaluation of comparison data.

If pupils select D for the highest yield, cover the yield column and read the damage rule aloud, then uncover it to compare both. If pupils say all offspring improve, use Q’s damage6 as the counterexample.
A close-relative risk discussion concerns the fictitious crop families only. Do not ask pupils for personal family, health or ancestry disclosures.
